FOR YOU

Here is what the clinician's plan says, in plain words.

Claim: Adding ultrasound to mammography screening is linked to fewer interval cancers (cancers found between regular screening visits) than mammography alone. The evidence for this is high-certainty.

What this means for you: your care team wants to talk with you about this result in light of your breast density and your personal risk. They also want to confirm with you what your screening schedule and follow-up plan should be. Please bring any questions to that conversation.

[source: pmid:34406400; pmid:30882843]

FOR YOU: After your pancreas surgery, the team has a choice of two ways to reconnect the pancreas: pancreatojejunostomy (PJ) or pancreatogastrostomy (PG). Based on the studies reviewed, the length of your hospital stay is probably the same with either method, but the evidence is low certainty. Your surgeon will choose based on things like their experience and your body and health risks. Please ask your surgical team and check the current hospital protocol to confirm how long you can expect to stay.

Claim: Length of hospital stay is probably the same for PJ and PG, but the evidence is low certainty.
[source: pmid:16327486; pmid:19092337; pmid:7574936]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Using more protein in feeding may help head growth a little more than using less, but the evidence for this is very weak, so it is not proven.

Your care team will use this as a loose guide only. Your feeding plan will be chosen around your own needs, not on this idea alone.

What your team will do:
- Check how much protein you are getting now, and whether that is low or moderate for your baby's growth.
- Measure your baby's head size regularly, along with weight and length, to watch the trend.
- Talk with your family about how limited the evidence is. It does not clearly show a benefit.
- Review the feeding plan with the neonatal team if your baby's growth or head size falls off track.

If you have questions about feeding, please ask your care team.

[source: pmid:27801753; pmid:10838460; pmid:8906139]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team looked at the research on whether a drain should be placed after lymph nodes are removed from behind the abdominal lining (retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy). Here is what that research says and what it means for you.

Claim: In the two studies available, drains did not clearly lower the chance of a fluid collection forming (a lymphocyst) in the short term compared with having no drain. The evidence is moderate in certainty.

What this means:
- Whether you get a drain will not be chosen only because of these studies. Your surgeon will decide based on their experience, how much tissue was removed, and your own health risks.
- Both studies looked at women having surgery for gynecologic cancers. If you had a different type of cancer or surgery, the results may apply differently.
- Whether or not you have a drain, your care team will watch for signs of a lymphocyst. These include swelling in your belly or pelvis, pain, or swelling in your leg. Tell your team right away if you notice any of these.
- Because only two studies are available, this advice may change if newer or larger studies come out. Your team will review it when that happens.

[source: pmid:9190979; pmid:12214830]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Adding ultrasound to a mammogram finds more breast cancers than a mammogram alone. The evidence for this is high certainty.
[source: pmid:34406400; pmid:29571797; pmid:26549432; pmid:23465737; pmid:30882843]

- Screening with both a mammogram and an ultrasound finds more cancers than a mammogram by itself.
- Your doctor may suggest adding an ultrasound to your mammogram. The choice depends on things like how dense your breast tissue is and your overall breast cancer risk.
- This evidence only tells us how many cancers are found. It does not tell us how often the extra scan gives a false alarm or leads to extra tests that turn out to be nothing. Ask your doctor about those points before you decide.
- If you or your doctor need more detail for a particular group of people, the original studies can be checked directly.

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your care team has looked at the evidence on a medicine called a cholinesterase inhibitor for memory problems linked to MS. Based on this, it is reasonable to talk with your treating clinician about this option, with regular checks on how your thinking and memory change over time.

Claim: In people with MS, a clinician's impression of cognitive change was higher with cholinesterase inhibitors than with placebo. The certainty of this evidence is high. The studies looked at donepezil, a cholinesterase inhibitor, for memory problems in MS.

What this means for you:
- Your clinician will check whether your memory or thinking symptoms match those studied in these trials.
- Your neurologist can explain the expected benefit and the possible side effects of this medicine.
- If you start treatment, your clinician will record a starting assessment of your thinking and memory, then repeat it at follow-up so changes can be tracked.

[source: pmid:15534239; pmid:21519001]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: This note explains a possible change to your baby's feeding plan.

Claim: Moderate protein in feeds may lead to greater length growth than low protein in premature babies, but the evidence is low certainty.
[source: pmid:27801753; pmid:10838460; pmid:8906139]

What this means:
- Your baby's care team will check how much protein your baby gets now and whether that amount is low or moderate compared with the amounts used in these studies.
- If the team thinks a change may help, they will talk with you about the possible benefit for length growth. The studies do not show this clearly, so the team will explain how sure or unsure the evidence is.
- The team will track length, weight, and brain development together. These studies also looked at these areas, so they matter for the feeding decision.
- The studies mainly included babies under 1500 g (very low birth weight). The team will decide how well your baby fits those groups before using these results.
- The feeding plan will be reviewed again as new information becomes available.

Please ask your care team any questions you have about this plan.

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Placing a drain behind the abdominal lining during surgery does not change the long-term chance of forming a lymphocyst, which is a fluid collection that can build up after lymph nodes are removed. The evidence for this is high-certainty.

Your surgical team will decide whether to place a drain based on other factors, such as the surgeon's judgment, what they find during the operation, and other effects this research did not study. A drain will not be used mainly to lower the risk of a lymphocyst forming later, because drainage has not been shown to do that. Your surgeon will explain the reasons for their choice and answer your questions.

[source: pmid:17466514]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: After a pancreas operation, the surgeon has to reconnect the pancreas to the intestine or stomach. There are two common ways to do this: pancreatojejunostomy (PJ), which connects it to the small intestine, and pancreatogastrostomy (PG), which connects it to the stomach. Based on the research reviewed, neither way has clearly been shown to lower the chance of a leak from the pancreas (called a pancreatic fistula) more than the other. The evidence for this is weak, so the answer is not certain.

Your surgical team will choose the method based on factors such as the surgeon's experience and the details of your anatomy. The research reviewed here does not cover those factors.

Claim: Overall postoperative pancreatic fistula risk is probably no different between PJ and PG, but the certainty of the evidence is low.

[source: pmid:24467711; pmid:16327486; pmid:15910726; pmid:19092337; pmid:24264781; pmid:25799130; pmid:26135690; pmid:23643139; pmid:7574936]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Ghrelin may increase how much food people eat compared with a placebo (a dummy treatment). This is based on only one small, short study in cancer patients who had lost their appetite, and the evidence is very low certainty, so this result is tentative.

What this means for you:

- This is one early study. It looked at a short period of time in cancer patients with poor appetite. Results like this are not yet proof that the treatment works or is safe.
- Please do not start ghrelin, or change your appetite treatment, based on this finding alone. Your care team will talk through it with you and check whether it applies to your situation.
- Doctors will look for larger or longer studies, and reviews that combine many studies, before drawing firm conclusions.
- In the meantime, your team will keep track of your appetite, how much you are eating, and your weight as part of your usual care.

If you have questions about this, please ask your care team.

[source: pmid:15181065]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your clinician is planning screening for you based on the fact that you have dense breasts. Here is what this means.

Claim: For women with dense breasts, adding an ultrasound to a mammogram finds more breast cancers than a mammogram alone.

- Your most recent mammogram report lists a breast density category. Your clinician will check this.
- Adding an ultrasound to your mammogram finds more cancers than a mammogram alone in dense breasts. The research supports this with high certainty.
- Your clinician will talk with you about whether to add an ultrasound to your screening plan. Your choice will be recorded.
- This research only looks at how many cancers are found. It does not tell us about false alarms, or whether lives are saved. Please ask your clinician about these points when you talk together.

[source: pmid:34406400; pmid:29571797; pmid:23116728; pmid:26549432]

FOR YOU: Your doctor wants to talk with you about cholinesterase inhibitors, a type of medicine that some people try for memory problems. Studies that compared these medicines with a dummy pill (placebo) in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) have not clearly shown whether the medicine changes how people feel their own memory is working. Two studies of donepezil, one of these medicines, reported better memory, but the evidence does not settle whether that applies to what people say about their own memory. So the benefit is uncertain, and it is wise to keep your expectations realistic.

If you and your doctor decide to try treatment, you can help by tracking your memory concerns over time and comparing them with a standard memory test. Your doctor will also review all your medicines and watch for side effects, both before you start and while you take it. The plan will be reviewed when new evidence is available.

Claim: The effect of cholinesterase inhibitors compared with placebo on patient self-reported memory change in MS is uncertain, although the certainty of the evidence is rated high.
